subsystems.name: Magnetic extraction array
subsystems.role: giant superconducting coils placed near the star's poles, creating a magnetic funnel that guides stellar-wind plasma into a controlled stream instead of letting it blow away evenly.
parts: power supply fed from the star or from beamed energy

subsystems.name: Plasma channel
subsystems.role: a magnetic nozzle or tether that carries captured plasma away from the star along a defined path, without it touching any solid surface.
parts: field coils spaced along the channel

subsystems.name: Collection station
subsystems.role: a receiving facility at a safer distance where the plasma is slowed, cooled and turned into storable material.
parts: cryogenic tanks for hydrogen and helium

subsystems.name: Separation and refining
subsystems.role: the star's output is mostly hydrogen and helium; heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen, iron and rare metals are trace components that must be concentrated.

subsystems.name: Mass transport
subsystems.role: moves extracted material to wherever it is needed — orbital construction sites, habitats or terraforming projects.

subsystems.name: Star-side control and safety
subsystems.role: monitors the star's magnetic activity and the extraction process, so the star is not destabilised and any inhabited planets are not harmed.

buildSteps.title: Map the star in detail
buildSteps.detail: Decades of remote observation of the star's magnetic cycle, corona and wind, plus modelling of how a magnetic array would perturb them. The Sun's wind already carries roughly 1–2 million tonnes of plasma per second at 300–800 km/s, so the raw material exists; the problem is concentrating it.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate magnetic scooping locally
buildSteps.detail: In space near a planet, build a small coil array and show that a magnetic field can deflect and funnel a tenuous plasma stream. Away from the star, the ram pressure of a wind is weak — a field of only tens of nanotesla matters at Earth's distance — so the first experiments are modest.

buildSteps.title: Scale up the field and move it inward
buildSteps.detail: Closer to the star the plasma is denser and hotter, so the coils and their cooling become far larger. This is the step where engineering leaves anything currently possible: field forces and heat loads grow by orders of magnitude.

buildSteps.title: Build the extraction array
buildSteps.detail: Place rings of superconducting coils around the star's polar regions, where the magnetic field naturally opens outward, and tune them to form a funnel. Any material near the star must survive intense radiation and heat, so the array is likely built and serviced from a distance by robots.

buildSteps.title: Build the collection station
buildSteps.detail: At a convenient distance, construct a facility that intercepts the channelled plasma, converts its kinetic energy into heat and electricity, and cools it into liquid hydrogen and helium. Rejecting that waste heat requires radiators of enormous area.

buildSteps.title: Separate the trace elements
buildSteps.detail: The collected gas is mostly hydrogen and helium. Mining useful metals means processing immense volumes of plasma for the small fraction of heavier nuclei, so this step is the main determinant of whether star lifting is worthwhile.

buildSteps.title: Establish transport
buildSteps.detail: Mass drivers or plasma thrusters push the refined material along routes to construction sites and settlements. Removing mass from a star also removes energy from its gravitational well, so the whole system needs a power budget measured in stellar fractions.

buildSteps.title: Operate, then expand
buildSteps.detail: Run the array for centuries to millennia, monitoring the star's behaviour and scaling extraction up or down. Even a very ambitious programme would remove only a tiny fraction of a star's mass over millions of years.

prerequisites.why: large fields at manageable cooling are essential for funnelling plasma; current magnets work at laboratory and industrial scale, not at stellar scale.
no project has assembled structures kilometres to thousands of kilometres across, with the robotics and materials that would need.
every step — capturing plasma, cooling it, separating it — produces waste heat that has nowhere to go in vacuum except by radiation.
we understand the sun's wind and corona in outline, but not well enough to predict how a large artificial field would reshape them.

prerequisites.tech: Autonomous robotics at extreme radiation and temperature
prerequisites.why: equipment placed near a star cannot be maintained by people; today's robots handle far milder conditions.

pathway.milestone: solar-wind and stellar-wind science from spacecraft; laboratory plasma experiments
pathway.unlocks: the basic data on how much material a star gives away and how it behaves.

pathway.milestone: in-space magnetic plasma experiments and large solar-wind sails or collectors
pathway.unlocks: proof that fields can steer a plasma stream in practice.

pathway.milestone: a working magnetic extraction array at one star, with collection and separation infrastructure
pathway.unlocks: industrial-scale access to hydrogen, helium and trace metals without digging them out of a planet.

pathway.milestone: routine stellar extraction, possibly as part of building habitats or moving a solar system's resources
pathway.unlocks: material supply for civilisation-scale engineering, with the caveat that the star and its planets must remain stable.
